meta.title: Who really told the Socrates "triple filter test" story? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The triple filter test — is it true, is it good, is it useful — has no classical source. It is absent from Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and Diogenes Laërtius. It circulates as a moral tale in German as 'Die drei Siebe' and in Ottoman tradition under Nasreddin Hodja's name.
meta.ogTitle: Who really told the Socrates 'triple filter test' story?
meta.ogDescription: Nobody in antiquity. The three-filters anecdote appears in no ancient text at all; it is a moral tale that travels under several wise men's names, Socrates being the most profitable.

answer.label: Not Socrates — a moral tale with no classical source
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · a travelling folk anecdote, no ancient source located
answer.sourceLine: The anecdote — a man arrives with gossip, Socrates stops him and asks whether the story passes three filters: truth, goodness, usefulness — appears in no ancient text whatsoever. Socrates wrote nothing, so it would have to be in Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes or Diogenes Laërtius. It is in none of the four. It is a travelling moral tale: German-speaking sources tell it as Die drei Siebe, ‘the three sieves,’ and Ottoman tradition tells a version under the name of Nasreddin Hodja. Socrates is a coat of paint, not the origin.
answer.confidenceText: A good story. Just not a Greek one.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Before you tell me, let the story pass three filters. The first is truth: are you certain that what you are about to tell me is true? The second is goodness: is it something good? The third is usefulness: will it be useful to me?
trail: The four-source test settles it. Socrates left no writings, so a story about Socrates has to be told by Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes or Diogenes Laërtius — the last of whom made a career of collecting exactly this kind of philosophical anecdote and quip. None of them tells it. If Diogenes Laërtius had known this story, he would have used it; it is precisely his sort of material.

The tale is older than the Socrates label but younger than Socrates. German-language reference sources circulate it as Die drei Siebe des Sokrates, and note that Ottoman writings tell a version of the same test under the name of the wise fool Nasreddin Hodja the German tradition ↗. A story that changes its sage as it crosses a border is folklore, not testimony.

In English it spread mostly as a forwarded email in the early 2000s, and its phrasing shows it: the vocabulary and sentence rhythm are modern English, not a translation from Greek. We could not establish a first printed appearance, and we are not going to invent one.
source.excerptNote: The core of the anecdote as it travels today, in the form you will meet it on social media. It is a genuinely useful test — and it is worth noticing that the third filter, usefulness, quietly does most of the work, since almost no gossip survives it.

source.rightsNote: Rights are indeterminate, so we make no claim. The anecdote has no identified author and no established date or place of first publication, which means its copyright status cannot be resolved — and any particular retelling you find online is its own author’s text. The underlying story appears to be old folklore in the public domain; a given modern wording of it may not be. Retell it in your own words and attribute it as an anonymous tale. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Socrates
author.bio: Socrates is the patron saint of the awkward question, so a story in which a man is stopped mid-gossip and interrogated about his own premises sounds exactly like him. It is also the reason the label sticks: he wrote nothing, and the four writers who transmit him disagree with each other enough that readers assume there must be more out there. There is not. The corpus is closed, and this story is not in it — which is why the same tale is told of Nasreddin Hodja wherever Socrates is not the local byword for wisdom.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is an anecdote rather than a sentence, which is why it slips past people: nobody thinks to fact-check a story the way they would fact-check a quotation. The result is a tale told about a real man that never happened.

items.why: Absent from Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and Diogenes Laërtius — the only four routes by which anything about Socrates reaches us. Diogenes Laërtius in particular collected exactly this genre of anecdote and does not have it.

Ottoman tradition attaches a version of the three-filters test to Nasreddin Hodja. When the same tale is told about whichever wise man the audience already respects, that is the definition of folklore the German account ↗.

The wording that circulates in English reads as modern English prose, not as a translation from Greek, and spread widely through forwarded emails and then social media. No first printing has been identified.

German sources tell it as Die drei Siebe — sieves rather than filters — and use it as a schoolroom lesson about gossip. It is the same three questions in older clothing, and it is no better sourced to antiquity.

We found no earliest printed version, in any language, that we can stand behind. That gap is the honest state of the evidence, and we would rather leave it visible than fill it with a plausible-looking citation.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous moral tale with no source in antiquity. Socrates is the most commercially useful name to hang it on; Ottoman tradition hangs the same story on Nasreddin Hodja.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The test is genuinely good advice, which is the whole problem. Because it works — three questions, and almost nothing you were about to repeat survives them — people are disinclined to check whether the man credited with it ever said it.
It also flatters the teller. Repeating the story is a way of announcing that you do not repeat stories, which is a neat trick for an anecdote about gossip to pull off.
context.detailsSummary: Why the four-source rule is decisive here
detailsBody: Socrates published nothing in his lifetime and left no manuscripts.
Plato wrote him as the central speaker of the dialogues — philosophically rich, but shaped by Plato’s own purposes.
Xenophon, a soldier, gives a plainer and more practical Socrates in the Memorabilia.
Aristophanes lampooned him on stage in the Clouds while he was alive.
Diogenes Laërtius, writing centuries later, compiled the philosophers’ sayings, jokes and comebacks — the exact bin this story would sit in.
The three-filters tale is in none of them. There is no fifth source to appeal to.
context.pull: Tell the same story about whichever sage your audience respects, and you have folklore.
